When designing modern reactive microservices or robust REST APIs using Java, developers frequently interact with generic types such as Mono<List<T>> or Flux<ResponseEntity<User>>. However, the legacy design of Java's generics introduces strict limitations due to Type Erasure, leading to three fundamental restrictions: no primitives as type arguments, no instanceof checks with parameterized types, and no arrays of generics. These restrictions are not arbitrary compiler hurdles; they stem from the historic choice made during Java 5 to maintain binary compatibility with pre-existing bytecode while introducing parameterization.

In reactive and distributed API pipelines—especially when serializing JSON bodies via WebFlux or handling asynchronous payload streams—understanding these restrictions prevents runtime ClassCastExceptions and subtle type-safety bugs. Because the JVM discards generic type information at runtime, checking whether an object is an instanceof List<String> becomes logically impossible. Similarly, the runtime cannot allocate an array of a generic type like List<String>[] because arrays enforce runtime reification (they know and check their component type at runtime), whereas generics are completely erased. Furthermore, autobox overhead makes primitive types fundamentally incompatible with Java's pointer-based reference architecture required by generic collections and reactive wrapper types.

rows: Generics require object references; primitives live on stack or unboxed in arrays/heaps.
Forced to use wrapper types (Integer, Long), adding GC pressure in high-throughput reactive pipelines.
Type Erasure removes generic arguments at compile time (List<String> becomes raw List).
Cannot dynamically validate generic response bodies or payload wrappers using standard instanceof.
Arrays are reified and throw ArrayStoreException on invalid assignments; generics are non-reified.
Cannot instantiate generic arrays like Mono<String>[]; must use collections like List<Mono<String>> instead.

items: Type Erasure ensures that List<String> and List<Integer> both compile down to the raw type java.util.List in bytecode, meaning the runtime has zero knowledge of the type parameter T.

Array reification requires the runtime to enforce type safety during array store operations, which directly conflicts with the non-reified nature of erased generic types, resulting in a compile-time Generic Array Creation error.

Pattern matching and instanceof checks with generic types require unbounded wildcards (e.g., obj instanceof List<?>) because checking specific type parameters is mathematically impossible post-compilation.

parsed_answer.content: Senior Architect Gotcha: In Spring WebFlux applications, trying to pass generic type references (like List<User>) into reactive operators or deserialization utils often fails because Spring cannot inspect the erased type at runtime. Always use ParameterizedTypeReference<List<User>> instead of Class<List<User>> to allow Spring's infrastructure to safely reconstruct the generic signatures via anonymous subclassing.

title: Restrictions — no primitives, no instanceof with parameterized types, no arrays of generics
